core: Creative Commons (CC) as a set of standardized, free-to-use public copyright licenses that operate on top of existing copyright, letting a rights holder grant permissions in advance ('some rights reserved')
The four license elements: BY (Attribution), SA (ShareAlike), NC (NonCommercial), ND (NoDerivatives)
The six license combinations (CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-ND, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-NC-ND) and roughly how open each is along two axes: commercial use allowed? adaptations allowed?
CC0 as a public-domain dedication (a legal tool, not a license) and the Public Domain Mark (PDM) as a label for works already in the public domain
That CC licenses are irrevocable once granted and require the licensor to actually hold or be authorized over the copyright
How to attribute a CC-licensed work using the TASL approach: Title, Author, Source, License
Why 'Creative Commons' is not a synonym for 'public domain' or 'no restrictions'
supporting: That every current (4.0) CC license includes the BY/attribution condition, so all six require credit
That only CC BY and CC BY-SA (plus CC0/public domain) are approved for Free Cultural Works
That CC licenses depend on copyright to work and do not override fair use or other copyright exceptions
outOfScope: General copyright basics, fair use factors, the public-domain term of protection, and commercial/stock (rights-managed vs royalty-free) licensing (owned by the Copyright and Image Licensing topic)
Detailed legal-code walkthroughs or jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction analysis; this lesson is educational, not legal advice

claims.claim: Creative Commons licenses are standardized, free, public copyright licenses that a rights holder applies to their own work to grant the public a set of permissions in advance; they work on top of copyright rather than replacing it, and Creative Commons states that CC licenses are copyright licenses that depend on the existence of copyright to work.

There are four license elements that combine to form the licenses: BY (Attribution) requires that credit be given to the creator; SA (ShareAlike) requires that adaptations be shared under the same terms; NC (NonCommercial) permits only noncommercial use, meaning use not primarily intended for or directed toward commercial advantage or monetary compensation; and ND (NoDerivatives) permits no adaptations or derivatives of the work to be shared.

The elements combine into six licenses: CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-ND, CC BY-NC-SA, and CC BY-NC-ND. CC BY is the most permissive (any use, including commercial and adaptation, with attribution) and CC BY-NC-ND is the most restrictive (noncommercial, verbatim redistribution only, with attribution). Because every current 4.0 license includes the BY element, all six require attribution.

CC0 is not a license but a public-domain dedication: a universal legal tool that lets creators and rights holders waive all copyright and related rights in their own work to the fullest extent permitted by law. Because it changes the legal status of the work, only the rights holder can apply it.

The Public Domain Mark (PDM) is a label, not a legal tool; it is used to identify works that are already in the public domain worldwide (for example because copyright has expired), and anyone with reliable knowledge that a work is in the public domain can apply it. This differs from CC0, which a rights holder uses to place their own work into the public domain.

CC licenses are irrevocable: once a work has been published under a CC license, licensees may continue using it under the license terms for the duration of the applicable copyright. A licensor can stop distributing the work under the license going forward, but cannot pull back the rights already granted to existing users.

You should only apply a CC license to material you own or are otherwise authorized to license; applying a license to material you do not hold rights to is not permitted. This makes owning or controlling the copyright a precondition for using CC licenses.

Creative Commons recommends attributing a CC-licensed work using the TASL approach: give the Title, the Author, the Source (a link to the original), and the License (naming and linking the specific CC license). Attribution should be reasonable to the medium and include the relevant information the licensor supplied.

Creative Commons is not the same as 'public domain' or 'free of all restrictions': most CC licenses reserve some rights and impose conditions (at minimum attribution), so reuse is permitted only within the license terms. Only CC0 and works marked as public domain carry no such copyright conditions.
Only CC BY and CC BY-SA are approved for Free Cultural Works; the NonCommercial and NoDerivatives licenses restrict reuse enough that they are not considered 'free' or 'open' in that stricter sense.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How to rank the 'openness' of the middle four licenses (whether NC or ND is more restrictive) is not a single fixed order.
positions: Creative Commons presents the licenses on a spectrum from most to least permissive but frames the differences in terms of two independent conditions (commercial use and adaptations) rather than a strict single ranking.
Popular charts sometimes force a single linear ranking, which can misstate that NC and ND restrict different things.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Taught the spectrum using the two independent axes CC actually uses (Is commercial use allowed? Are adaptations allowed?), naming CC BY as most open and CC BY-NC-ND as most restrictive, and avoided asserting a precise linear rank for the middle licenses.

sourceRecords.title: About CC Licenses (Share Your Work)
sourceRecords.notes: Creative Commons's own description of the license system, from the organization that authors and stewards the licenses (the authoritative primary source). Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports: the four license elements and their exact definitions (BY 'credit must be given to you, the creator'; SA 'adaptations must be shared under the same terms'; NC 'only noncommercial use of your work is permitted... not primarily intended for or directed towards commercial advantage or monetary compensation'; ND 'no derivatives or adaptations of your work are permitted'); the six license combinations and their relative permissiveness from CC BY (most open) to CC BY-NC-ND (most restrictive); and that BY and BY-SA are the licenses approved for Free Cultural Works. creativecommons.org states site content is CC BY 4.0 unless noted; prose here is original and only short definitional phrases are quoted with attribution.

sourceRecords.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sourceRecords.notes: Creative Commons FAQ, read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports: CC licenses are irrevocable ('CC licenses are not revocable. Once something has been published under a CC license, licensees may continue using it according to the license terms for the duration of applicable copyright'), while a licensor may stop distributing going forward; that you must own or be authorized to license the material ('You should not apply a license to material that you do not own or that you are not authorized to license'); that CC licenses 'are copyright licenses, and depend on the existence of copyright to work' and do not override exceptions like fair use; and that CC0 is a public-domain dedication rather than a license. Original prose; short phrases quoted with attribution.

sourceRecords.title: Public Domain (CC0 and the Public Domain Mark)
sourceRecords.notes: Creative Commons public-domain tools page, read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports the CC0 vs Public Domain Mark distinction: CC0 is 'a universal legal tool that allows creators and rightsholders to waive all copyright and related rights in their works to the fullest extent permitted by law' and, because it changes the legal status of the work, 'can only be used by the rightsholder'; the Public Domain Mark 'is a label, not a legal tool... used to identify works already in the public domain worldwide' and can be applied by anyone with reliable knowledge that a work is in the public domain. Original prose; short phrases quoted with attribution.

sourceRecords.title: Best practices for attribution
sourceRecords.notes: Creative Commons wiki page on attribution, read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports the TASL approach — Title, Author, Source, License — as the recommended elements of a good attribution, with the model image example ('[work title] by [author] is licensed under [CC license with link]') and the principle that attribution must be reasonable to the medium and include the relevant information the licensor supplied. Title is required under CC 3.0 and earlier and optional under 4.0. Original prose; short phrases quoted with attribution.
